analysis.one_liner: Repeals the ACA's coverage expansion and replaces it with state high-risk pools and reinsurance grants.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed the ACA's coverage expansion and spent $25 billion on state high-risk pools and reinsurance instead, was referred to three House committees and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal Title I of the Affordable Care Act — the law's core coverage provisions, including its subsidies, insurance market rules, and Medicaid expansion — and bring back the pre-2010 rules insurers used to operate under. In its place, states could set up high-risk pools, reinsurance programs, or other plans for people with preexisting conditions, backed by a $25 billion federal appropriation and loss grants. A small federal fallback pool with $2.5 billion would cover people in states that never set up a program.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers gain the most: repeal would free them from the ACA's guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules and its other coverage requirements, while new state reinsurance programs would pay them back for covering high-cost patients. A narrower group — uninsured people with preexisting conditions — would get an access route through high-risk pools, but at premiums up to 150% of the standard market rate and with weaker benefits than the ACA offered. States would get federal seed grants of up to $5 million and reimbursement of pool and reinsurance losses.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA's coverage-expansion provisions (Title I of the ACA and related sections) and restores the laws they had replaced, freeing insurers from those requirements.

Lets states instead run qualified reinsurance programs or other 'innovative methods' that make federal reinsurance payments to, or otherwise limit the risk of, insurers covering high-cost individuals — with grants both for startup costs and for operating losses.

Rewrites the high-risk pool program with consumer protections: premiums capped at 150% of the state's average individual-market premium, no lifetime limits, guaranteed availability, and no waiting lists or waiting periods.
Appropriates $25 billion for the state pool, reinsurance, and innovative-method programs, plus $2.5 billion for a federal fallback pool in states that never set up their own program.

Includes anti-dumping provisions letting states sanction insurers that push sick people out of prior coverage and into the pool, and requiring insurers to reimburse the federal fallback pool for such cases.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the $25 billion appropriation and the loss grants, plus the $2.5 billion federal fallback pool. The larger cost falls on people who would have gotten ACA subsidies or Medicaid expansion coverage — they would lose both with nothing replacing them — and on people with preexisting conditions who stay outside the pools, since insurers could once again deny them coverage or charge them based on health status. Pool enrollees themselves would pay premiums of up to 150% of standard rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers; people losing ACA coverage and protections

drawbacks.text: Repeal would restore the pre-ACA legal landscape, in which insurers could deny coverage, exclude conditions, impose lifetime limits, and price policies based on health status — protections the bill replaces only for the narrower group of people eligible for the pools.

Only 'eligible individuals' — uninsured people with preexisting conditions, plus some people in the Medicare disability waiting period — qualify for the pools; the millions who would have received ACA subsidies or expanded Medicaid get no substitute.

Pool coverage would cost up to 150% of the standard individual-market premium, far more than the income-based subsidies the ACA provided, and the bill eliminates the bonus grants that had funded supplemental benefits for pool enrollees.

The $25 billion appropriation is small relative to the coverage expansion it would repeal, and the bill requires states to show a mechanism for continuing to fund pool losses after federal grants end — a long-term obligation states would bear.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insurers, the trade is clearly favorable: lighter regulatory obligations plus taxpayer-funded reinsurance for the high-cost customers they do keep. For patients, the bill offers a real but narrow lifeline — a premium-capped, guaranteed-access pool for people with preexisting conditions — while removing broader protections (subsidies, guaranteed issue for everyone, the Medicaid expansion) that reached many more people. Its own funding, $25 billion, is far smaller than the coverage expansion it repeals, so the honest conclusion is that the bill helps a modest group of sick individuals at the price of taking coverage and protections away from a much larger group, with insurers coming out ahead.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2012, sent to three House committees and their health subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on August 2, 2012, joined by original cosponsors Reps. Pete Sessions, Joe Barton, and Daniel Lungren.
The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees, and within weeks it was further referred to health subcommittees in each.
No committee ever held a markup or reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor; the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill still parked in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on the ACA's coverage expansions and insurance protections are better off, because the repeal never advanced; insurers did not get the lighter rules and reinsurance payments the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People protected by the ACA's coverage rules

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from the ACA's guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules and related coverage requirements, letting them price and deny coverage based on health status again. The bill then has taxpayers pay insurers reinsurance for the high-cost customers they do cover, so insurers shed risk while the public loses the protections that bound them.
Repealing the ACA's coverage expansion would leave more patients uninsured, shifting costs back onto hospitals and providers as uncompensated care. Providers and their patients lose together here.

industries.industry: State high-risk pool and reinsurance programs
industries.note: The bill channels $25 billion in federal money through state pools, reinsurance programs, and similar plans, including up to $5 million seed grants and reimbursement of operating losses. It entrenches state-run high-risk coverage as the substitute for the ACA's market rules, while giving the states running it a new funding stream.
